text: This is the last line of a message an AI is about to receive. Your action plan must strictly match sell. A workflow writes that line to hold a model to a verdict it has already been given. So, who decided the verdict? Let me take you to the meeting. Hi, this is Tanmay Kulkarni in for Humanitarian's AI. This week I contributed to Mycroft, a book in a working repository of finance pipelines. It calls them recipes. One of them, the would-be simulation agent, asks three different questions about a stock, then hands an AI the answers. Three voices, one written record, and one question for this whole video. Who had a vote and how

Much? My pull request, now merged, made the six steps before the AI runnable on test data with checks. Every company you'll see is invented and none of this is investment advice. Today's stock is Ironbridge Power, invented growth 5%, sentiment .35, a price-to-earnings of 80, and an aggressive investor. I'll call the workflow the chair and the three simulators its voices. The chair's first job is to make sure every seat has something to read. Ironbridge arrived with everything filled in, but if a request arrives with nothing, the chair fills every seat itself. A company called Unknown Company, growth 15%, sentiment .5. The meeting starts anyway. First voice, growth against sentiment.

It sorts a stock into one of nine boxes, low, medium, or high on each. Ironbridge is low and low. The voice says strong sell with 82% confidence. Second voice, the same stock judged for three kinds of investor. Conservative says avoid. Balanced says avoid. Aggressive has the loosest limits. Growth at least 5%, sentiment at least .35, price-to-earnings no more than 80, debt-to-equity no more than 1 and 1/2, and Ironbridge sits exactly on all four, four out of four, enter a full position. Third voice, and this one asks something different. Not what should we do, but how close is it to changing its mind? It nudges growth and sentiment up and down

Six ways and watches the verdict. Three of the six nudges change it. The stability score, 0.05 out of one. Now they disagree. The first voice says strong sell. The second says enter a full position. Nobody has made a mistake. They were asked different questions. So the chair weighs them 45, 35, and 20. The chair scale runs from one to five. Strong sell sits at the bottom and enter a full position at the top. So a smaller weight on the top can outweigh a bigger weight on the bottom. The voices contribute 0.37, 1.75, and 0.05. Together, 2.17 out of five. Anywhere from 1.8 to 2.8, the chair

Writes down a sell. Then the chair writes the minutes, about 470 words. The stock, each voice, the stress tests, the verdict, and one last instruction for someone who wasn't in the room. The action plan must strictly match sell. The AI only ever receives the minutes. And in the minutes, a number somebody typed looks exactly like a number the chair filled in. Here's where I got something wrong. To check the original, I wrote a second minute taker, a Python copy of those six steps, and ran both on the same meetings. On two requests, it wrote a different verdict. Those were requests where growth was typed as the letters A,

B, C, and sentiment was left as empty text. Python and JavaScript disagree about the smallest of a list when one entry isn't a number. I fixed it. Now both write the same minutes to the letter. On all 23 requests, and a test keeps that slip from coming back. Nothing was sent anywhere. The step that would call the AI in the step that would save the answer are written down as hand-offs marked not approved. Five items in the recipe are still open, and it still says draft on purpose. If an AI is going to summarize your next meeting, have you read the minutes? Who had a vote, and how much of one? A good
Answer names the voices and their weights. The AI will figure it out doesn't count. Adjourned. Tanmay Kulkarni, in for Humanitarian's AI, signing off.
